SWE.summary: Uppsala kings and regional assemblies inch toward Christian monarchy later than Denmark/Norway.
SWE.conflicts: Eastern Viking routes; Finnish coasts; Danish rivalry.
SWE.leaders: Olof Skötkonung (traditionally first Christian king); regional jarls.
SWE.religion: Pagan cult center at Uppsala persists in memory as baptism spreads unevenly.
SWE.culture: Mälaren valley power; runestones; trade toward Rus’.
SWE.story: Sweden’s conversion is slower and more regional — a reminder that ‘Viking Age’ is not one synchronized baptism.

ESP.name: Andalusi taifas & northern Christian kingdoms
ESP.summary: After Córdoba’s caliphal collapse, taifa courts glitter while León–Castile, Navarre, and Catalan counts advance.
ESP.conflicts: Fitna civil wars; Christian tribute systems (parias); shifting frontiers.
ESP.leaders: Almanzor (late caliphal memory); taifa kings of Seville/Toledo; Alfonso V of León; Sancho of Navarre.
ESP.religion: Islam in the south; Latin Christianity in the north; Jews as cultural brokers in both.
ESP.culture: Arabic poetry and science; Mozarabic Christians; Romanesque beginnings in the north.
ESP.story: The fall of the caliphate turns one of Europe’s richest courts into competing city-kingdoms — brilliance and vulnerability that Christian kings exploit through parias and siege.

PRT.name: County of Portugal
PRT.summary: A frontier county of León on the Atlantic edge of the Reconquista, not yet a fully independent kingdom (that crystallizes in the 12th century).
PRT.conflicts: Raids vs Andalusi neighbors; loyalty politics toward León.
PRT.leaders: Counts of Portugal under León’s shadow (e.g. Menendo González era memory; later Henry of Burgundy still ahead).
PRT.culture: Atlantic agrarian frontier; pilgrimage roads beginning to matter.
PRT.story: Portugal’s later independence is seeded in this county’s frontier identity — a small Christian lordship facing the taifa world.

ITA.name: Imperial Italy, Rome, Byzantine & Islamic south
ITA.summary: North and center: emperors, popes, and cities; south: Byzantines and Muslim Sicily before Norman conquest.
ITA.conflicts: Crescentii/ Tusculani Roman factions; imperial–papal tension; Arab raids.
ITA.leaders: Ottonian emperors in Italy; popes of the age; Byzantine catepans; Kalbid emirs in Sicily.
ITA.religion: Latin Christianity vs Greek Orthodoxy vs Islam on one peninsula.
ITA.culture: Manuscript centers; early communal stirrings; Mediterranean trade of Amalfi/Venice.
ITA.story: Italy at the millennium is Europe’s religious crossroads — three civilizations on one boot — soon to be remade by Norman adventurers.

POL.name: Piast Poland
POL.summary: Mieszko I’s baptism (966) and Bolesław Chrobry’s kingship place Poland inside Latin Christendom’s political club.
POL.conflicts: Wars with the Reich, Bohemia, and Kievan Rus’; pagan reaction crises.
POL.leaders: Mieszko I; Bolesław I the Brave; early Piast bishops.
POL.religion: Latin Christianity newly established; pagan uprisings still possible.
POL.culture: Gniezno as sacral center; warrior-duke retinues; missionary politics.
POL.story: The Gniezno meeting (1000) with Otto III becomes Poland’s foundational European recognition scene — crown, relics, and imperial friendship as statecraft.

HUN.name: Árpád Hungary under Stephen I
HUN.summary: Magyar dukes become a Christian kingdom; Stephen’s crown binds the Carpathian basin to Latin Europe.
HUN.conflicts: Internal conversion conflicts; German and Polish neighbor politics; steppe remnant pressures.
HUN.leaders: Géza; Stephen I (St Stephen); early queens and German alliances.
HUN.religion: Forced and negotiated Christianization; dioceses founded; pagan revolts later in the century.
HUN.culture: Nomad-origin elite adopting European kingship; Latin clergy; county administration beginnings.
HUN.story: Stephen’s crown (sent from the pope in tradition) is Hungary’s origin myth of Christian statehood — a steppe people choosing Latin Europe.

UKR.name: Kievan Rus’
UKR.summary: Vladimir’s baptism aligns Rus’ with Byzantine Orthodoxy; Kiev sits on the Dnieper trade route ‘from the Varangians to the Greeks.’
UKR.conflicts: Pecheneg wars; succession among Rurikid princes; Byzantine alliance and friction.
UKR.leaders: Vladimir the Great; Yaroslav the Wise (rising); Varangian retinues.
UKR.religion: Byzantine Orthodox conversion; earlier pagan and diverse faiths among elites.
UKR.culture: Church Slavonic literacy; Scandinavian-Slavic elite fusion; iconic church building.
UKR.story: The Primary Chronicle’s tale of choosing a faith — testing Islam, Judaism, Western and Eastern Christianity — is literary statecraft: Orthodoxy as civilizational choice.

RUS.name: Northern Rus’ & Novgorod orbit
RUS.summary: Forest towns and river routes of northern Rus’ linked to Kiev’s federation and Scandinavian trade.
RUS.conflicts: Tribute politics among tribes and princes; eastern Finnish/Uralic neighbors.
RUS.leaders: Local Rurikid princes; Novgorod posadnik traditions forming.
RUS.religion: Christianization spreading north from Kiev unevenly.
RUS.culture: Fur trade; wooden towns; bilingual contact zones.
RUS.story: Novgorod’s later republican myth has roots in this river-road world where merchants and princes bargain under loose Kievan suzerainty.

GRC.name: Byzantine Empire (Macedonian apex)
GRC.summary: Basil II’s Byzantium is a military and fiscal superpower reclaiming the Balkans and projecting into the Caucasus and Italy.
GRC.conflicts: Bulgarian wars; Fatimid frontier; internal court factions.
GRC.leaders: Basil II; Constantine VIII; military aristocracy.
GRC.religion: Greek Orthodoxy as imperial ideology; missionary work among Slavs.
GRC.culture: Macedonian Renaissance learning; Constantinople’s ceremonial majesty.
GRC.story: Basil’s blinding of Bulgarian captives (as told) is the dark legend of reconquest — empire restored by terror and administration.

BGR.name: First Bulgarian Empire (final phase)
BGR.summary: Samuel’s Bulgaria fights Basil II until catastrophic defeat and Byzantine annexation.
BGR.conflicts: Existential war with Byzantium; shifting capitals and mountain resistance.
BGR.religion: Slavic Orthodoxy with Bulgarian patriarchal memory.
BGR.culture: Slavic liturgy; fortress warfare in the western Balkans.
BGR.story: The end of the First Empire becomes a national epic of resistance — historically a Byzantine reconquest that remaps the Balkans for generations.

periods.label: High Medieval
periods.narrative: High Medieval Christendom: Capetians, Plantagenets, Holy Roman Empire, Italian communes, Reconquista vs Nasrid Granada, Byzantine twilight and Balkan kingdoms, Rus’ under Golden Horde pressure. Vernacular literatures mature. Genetic geography is largely set; mobility and colonization (Ostsiedlung, crusading, trade) tweak edges.
periods.culturesNote: HRE, Capetian France, Plantagenet realms, communal Italy, Iberian kingdoms/Granada, Balkan states, Rus’ principalities/Golden Horde.

iberia.description: Las Navas de Tolosa breaks Almohad hegemony; Castile and Aragon expand; Portugal consolidates Atlantic independence; Granada endures as Islam’s last peninsula foothold. Toledo’s translation culture, military orders, and convivencia under strain shape society. Demography mixes Christian northerners, Andalusi Muslims, and Jews — politics of conquest and confession on medieval Iberian ancestries.
iberia.languages: Castilian, Portuguese, Catalan, etc.; Andalusi Arabic; Basque; Latin/Hebrew in domains
iberia.linguisticNote: Romance victory narrative with lasting Arabic loanwords and toponyms.
iberia.ancestryNote: Shifting clines from medieval contact; post-conquest homogenization incomplete.

britain.description: Norman conquest installs a French-speaking military elite atop an English population; by 1200 the Angevin/Plantagenet realm ties England to half of France until Capetian reconquest. Magna Carta politics, common-law growth, Gothic cathedrals, and crusading culture define the age. Wales faces Edwardian conquest later in the century; Scotland fights for independence; Ireland’s lordship remains incomplete. Genetics: elite Norman input on an early medieval English majority — institutions and language contact change faster than deep ancestry.
britain.languages: Middle English; Anglo-Norman French; Welsh/Gaelic/Scots/etc.; Latin
britain.linguisticNote: Trilingual elite culture; English re-emerges as state language later.
britain.ancestryNote: Elite Norman layer; majority continuity from early medieval England.

france.description: Capetian kings from Philip Augustus onward turn a sacred demesne into a territorial state: Normandy seized, Languedoc crushed in the Albigensian Crusade, Louis IX’s holy monarchy, Paris university theology. Gothic architecture radiates from Île-de-France. Occitan culture suffers political defeat without total demographic replacement. Ancestry remains medieval French continua under intensifying royal fiscal-military power.
france.languages: Old/Middle French; Occitan; Breton; Basque edge; Latin
france.linguisticNote: Langue d’oïl vs oc is a major internal linguistic divide.
france.ancestryNote: Medieval France continuity; north/south structure persists.

central.description: The Hohenstaufen drama, elective empire, eastward German settlement (Ostsiedlung), Přemyslid/Luxemburg Bohemia, and Piast Poland’s fragmentation-and-reunion fill Central Europe. Towns under Magdeburg law, Minnesang, and crusading orders on the Baltic define culture. Genetics track medieval German, Slavic, and Magyar continua with settler mobility — not a new deep component.
central.languages: Middle High German; Czech/Polish/etc.; Italian vernaculars; Latin; Hungarian in the basin
central.linguisticNote: Empire ≠ one language; Latin and German as linking codes.
central.ancestryNote: German–Slavic contact zones show admixture; alpine/italian lands differ.

scandinavia.description: Christian kingdoms of Denmark, Norway, and Sweden integrate into Latin Europe: archbishoprics, written laws, crusades toward Finland and the eastern Baltic. Old Norse literary culture flowers in Icelandic manuscripts. Ancestry is Nordic medieval continuity after Viking-Age consolidations.
scandinavia.linguisticNote: From Old Norse relative unity to separate medieval standards.
scandinavia.ancestryNote: Continuous with Viking Age Nordic ternary; Christian medieval kingdoms are political-cultural, not a new genetic pulse.

italy.description: Communal cities, papal monarchy, Frederick II’s Sicilian state, and maritime republics (Venice, Genoa) make Italy Europe’s political laboratory. Mendicant orders remake piety; universities and vernacular poetry rise toward Dante. Ancestry: Italian medieval urban–rural mixes with Mediterranean trade contacts.
italy.languages: Italian dialects/volgare; Latin; Greek remnants in south
italy.linguisticNote: Dante’s era crystallizes literary Italian on a dialect continuum.
italy.ancestryNote: Ports cosmopolitan; hinterlands more local medieval Italian.

balkans.description: Byzantium’s Komnenian then Palaiologan struggles; Second Bulgarian Empire; Serbian rise under Nemanjići; Hungarian oversight in Croatia. Orthodox and Catholic frontiers harden. Genetics: Balkan medieval continua; the story is empire, schism, and Slavic kingship.
balkans.languageFamily: South Slavic + Greek + Albanian (emerging in record)
balkans.languages: Serbian/Bulgarian/etc.; Greek; Albanian; Romance islands; Latin in Catholic zones
balkans.linguisticNote: Medieval Balkan multilingualism before Ottoman overlay.
balkans.ancestryNote: Microregional mosaics; schematic continuity with early medieval Balkans.

eastern.culture: Rus’ principalities under Golden Horde pressure
eastern.description: Kievan Rus’ fragments under princely feuds then Mongol conquest (1237–40); successor principalities and the Golden Horde reorders the east; Lithuania expands into Ruthenian lands. Church Slavonic culture persists under steppe suzerainty. Deep ancestry unchanged in kind; political gravity shifts toward Moscow and Vilnius later.
eastern.languages: Old East Slavic varieties; Turkic; Mongol administration languages
eastern.linguisticNote: Court multilingualism over East Slavic countryside.
eastern.ancestryNote: Medieval East Slavic base + variable steppe/Mongol-era input.

periods.linguistics: Medieval vernaculars (French, Middle English, MHG, Italian volgare, Castilian, etc.) plus Latin as learned lingua franca; Greek east; Arabic/Hebrew in Iberia; Turkic/Mongol court languages on the steppe edge.

FIN.name: Swedish realm in Finland
FIN.summary: Swedish crusades/colonization into Finnish lands; local Finnish societies under expanding Swedish rule.
FIN.conflicts: Conflict with Novgorod for Karelia/eastern Finland; internal incorporation of Finnish tribes into Swedish law and Church.
FIN.leaders: Swedish regents and bishops directing Finnish crusades/colonization.
FIN.religion: Latin Christianity spreading among Finnish societies under Swedish rule.
FIN.culture: Coastal Swedish law towns; inland Finnish agrarian societies.
FIN.story: The ‘Finnish crusades’ are conquest-and-conversion stories — Sweden’s eastern realm built by cross and castle.

SWE.name: Kingdom of Sweden
SWE.conflicts: Rivalry with Denmark and Norway; eastern wars vs Novgorod; Finnish expansion.
SWE.leaders: Eric dynasty / Folkung kings (e.g. Birger Jarl’s era in the long 13th c.).
SWE.culture: Landscape laws; castle building; Finnish expansion.
SWE.story: Birger Jarl becomes the realm-builder of later Swedish memory — Stockholm’s founding legend and eastern crusade politics.

DNK.name: Kingdom of Denmark
DNK.summary: Valdemar-age Danish power in the Baltic.
DNK.conflicts: Wars with Wends, Holstein, Norway/Sweden; Baltic crusading politics.
DNK.religion: Latin Christian monarchy with strong episcopal partners.
DNK.culture: Baltic crusading; brick Romanesque/Gothic; Law of Jutland.
DNK.story: Absalon and the Valdemars turn Denmark into a Baltic crusader kingdom — priest and king as twin founders.

NOR.name: Kingdom of Norway
NOR.conflicts: Civil wars earlier; interest in Isles; Danish rivalry.
NOR.religion: Latin Christianity; church–crown civil wars earlier in the century.
NOR.culture: King’s sagas; coastal trade; North Atlantic isles.
NOR.story: The civil-war age ends in Håkon’s European-style kingship — Norway briefly looks like a high-medieval state among peers.

ISL.name: Icelandic Commonwealth
ISL.summary: Godar chieftaincy republic with Althing; Norwegian royal pressure rising by the 13th c.
ISL.conflicts: Sturlung Age feuds; later submission to Norway (1262).
ISL.leaders: Goðar chieftains; Snorri Sturluson in the Sturlung arc.
ISL.culture: Saga writing — Europe’s great vernacular prose laboratory.
ISL.story: The sagas invent a nation’s memory in prose while the commonwealth kills itself into Norwegian rule.

GBR.name: Plantagenet England
GBR.conflicts: Wars in France (Angevin lands); Welsh/Scottish wars; baronial conflict.
GBR.leaders: Henry II; Eleanor of Aquitaine; Richard I; John; Edward I (later in the long high-medieval arc).
GBR.religion: Latin Christianity; Becket conflict as church-vs-crown archetype; Jewish communities until 1290 expulsion.
GBR.culture: Angevin law (common law beginnings); Gothic cathedrals; Arthurian romance fashion; Magna Carta politics.
GBR.story: Becket’s murder in Canterbury (1170) and Magna Carta (1215) become England’s twin stories of sacred blood and baronial bridle on kings.

IRL.name: Lordship of Ireland / Gaelic Ireland
IRL.summary: English lordship in Pale vs Gaelic kingdoms.
IRL.conflicts: Continual frontier war between Anglo-Norman lords and Gaelic polities.
IRL.leaders: English justiciars; Gaelic kings; Anglo-Norman lords (de Burgh, Fitzgerald beginnings).
IRL.religion: Latin Christian; reforming church under English and papal pressure.
IRL.culture: Hybrid marcher culture; bardic learning; castle and tower houses.
IRL.story: Strongbow’s century-old invasion settles into unfinished conquest — England’s oldest overseas entanglement.

FRA.name: Capetian France
FRA.summary: Philip Augustus consolidating the domaine royal.
FRA.conflicts: Wars with Plantagenets/England; Albigensian Crusade in the south; Flemish conflicts.
FRA.leaders: Philip II Augustus; Louis IX (St Louis); Philip IV the Fair.
FRA.religion: Catholic monarchy; Albigensian Crusade in the south; university theology in Paris.
FRA.culture: Gothic invention (Saint-Denis to Chartres); troubadour/trouvère song; royal bureaucracy.
FRA.story: Philip Augustus wins Bouvines (1214) and takes Normandy — Capetian France becomes a real territorial kingdom, not only a sacred title.

DEU.name: Holy Roman Empire (German lands)
DEU.summary: Hohenstaufen imperial politics; princes and cities.
DEU.conflicts: Investiture aftershocks; Italian campaigns; Slavic eastern frontier (Ostsiedlung).
DEU.leaders: Frederick Barbarossa; Frederick II; elective princes.
DEU.religion: Catholic empire; investiture aftershocks; crusading emperors.
DEU.culture: Minnesang; Kaiser myth; Italian–German political double life.
DEU.story: Barbarossa’s legend — drowned on crusade, sleeping in a mountain in folklore — outlives the political failure to fully master Italy.

CZE.name: Přemyslid Bohemia
CZE.summary: Kingdom within the Empire; Prague as a rising central European capital.
CZE.conflicts: Imperial politics; Hungarian and Polish wars; Ottokar’s later expansion and fall.
CZE.leaders: Přemyslid kings; Ottokar II ('Iron and Gold') in the 13th c. climax.
CZE.culture: Courtly culture; German settlement in towns; Gothic beginnings.
CZE.story: Ottokar’s rise and Rudolf of Habsburg’s victory (1278) shift Central Europe’s crown toward Habsburg destiny.

POL.name: Fragmented Poland
POL.conflicts: Teutonic Knights on the Baltic; Bohemian/Hungarian neighbors; Mongol invasion (1241).
POL.leaders: High medieval Piasts; fragmentation among duchies then reunification under Władysław Łokietek / Casimir the Great (long arc).
POL.religion: Latin Christianity; monastic orders; Jewish settlement invited in law (Casimir tradition).
POL.story: Casimir the Great’s later reputation — ‘found Poland of wood, left it of stone’ — crowns the high-medieval Polish arc.

LTU.name: Grand Duchy of Lithuania
LTU.summary: Pagan Lithuanian expansion under early Gediminids’ precursors.
LTU.conflicts: Wars with Teutonic/Livonian Orders; Ruthenian expansion; Polish entanglement later.
LTU.leaders: Mindaugas (crowned king 1253); early Gediminid predecessors later.
LTU.religion: Pagan Lithuania resisting Teutonic baptism-by-sword — conversion still ahead.
LTU.culture: Baltic warrior dukedom expanding into Rus’ lands.
LTU.story: Mindaugas’s brief crown is Lithuania’s paradoxical debut: a pagan power baptized for politics, then murdered back into myth.

HUN.name: Kingdom of Hungary
HUN.summary: Árpád Hungary as a major Central European power.
HUN.conflicts: Mongol devastation (1241); Balkan and Austrian frontier wars.
HUN.leaders: Béla III; Andrew II (Golden Bull 1222); Béla IV after the Mongol invasion.
HUN.religion: Latin Christian realm; Orthodox and steppe minorities.
HUN.story: The Mongol invasion (1241) burns the kingdom; Béla IV’s stone-castle program is Hungary’s rebirth story.

ESP.name: Castile & Aragon
ESP.conflicts: Wars with Almohads/Nasrids; rivalry between Castile and Aragon; Portuguese independence path.
ESP.leaders: Alfonso VIII of Castile; James I of Aragon; Ferdinand III; Nasrid founders in Granada.
ESP.religion: Reconquista Catholicism; Islam in Al-Andalus; Jewish Golden Age fading under pressure.
ESP.culture: Toledo translation networks; Cantigas; military orders (Santiago, Calatrava).
ESP.story: Las Navas de Tolosa (1212) breaks Almohad power — the hinge battle of the Iberian Middle Ages.

PRT.name: Kingdom of Portugal
PRT.summary: Afonsine Portugal after recognition of sovereignty.
PRT.conflicts: Wars with Castile and Muslim south; Atlantic orientation beginning.
PRT.leaders: Afonso I; Sancho I; Afonso II/III in the long Reconquista arc.
PRT.culture: Atlantic frontier kingdom; Burgundian dynasty founding myths.
PRT.story: Ourique and papal recognition stories invent Portugal as a crusader kingdom distinct from León–Castile.

ITA.name: Communal Italy / southern kingdoms
ITA.conflicts: Guelf–Ghibelline wars; imperial–papal conflict; Venetian–Byzantine rivalry.
ITA.leaders: Frederick II in the south; papal rivals; Venetian doges; communal podestà.
ITA.religion: Papacy at the height of claims; mendicant orders (Francis, Dominic).
ITA.culture: Communal towers; early universities; vernacular poetry toward Dante.
ITA.story: Francis of Assisi’s renunciation and the mendicant revolution remake popular piety from Umbrian roads to European cities.

GRC.name: Frankish Greece / Byzantine remnant
GRC.leaders: Byzantine emperors of Nicaea then restored Palaiologoi; Latin emperors in the interlude.
GRC.culture: Exile courts; fragmented Greek lordships; Venetian ports.
GRC.story: The Fourth Crusade’s sack of Constantinople (1204) is Byzantium’s trauma — Christian conquest of the Christian capital.

BGR.name: Second Bulgarian Empire
BGR.conflicts: Wars with Byzantium/Latins; Hungarian and Serbian neighbors.
BGR.leaders: Asen dynasty of the Second Bulgarian Empire; Kaloyan; Ivan Asen II.
BGR.religion: Bulgarian Orthodoxy; temporary union politics with Rome.
BGR.culture: Tarnovo as ‘third Rome’ claim; fortress churches.
BGR.story: The uprising of the Asens restores Bulgarian empire between Byzantium and Hungary — a Balkan renaissance of arms.

SRB.name: Serbian lands
SRB.conflicts: Expansion vs Byzantium/Bulgaria; later empire under Dušan (13th–14th c. arc).
SRB.leaders: Stefan Nemanja; St Sava; Stefan Dušan (14th c. culmination of the arc).
SRB.religion: Autocephalous Serbian Orthodoxy forged by Sava.
SRB.culture: Hilandar monastery; law codes; hill-fort capitals.
SRB.story: St Sava — prince turned archbishop — is Serbia’s culture hero of church and letters.

TUR.name: Byzantine / Turkish Anatolia
TUR.summary: After Manzikert (1071) Anatolia becomes a Seljuk–Byzantine contest; crusaders cut through.
TUR.conflicts: Seljuk sultanate of Rum; crusader corridors; Byzantine recovery attempts.
TUR.leaders: Komnenian emperors; Seljuk sultans of Konya.
TUR.religion: Greek Orthodoxy vs advancing Islam in Anatolia.
TUR.culture: Frontier emirates; still-Byzantine coasts and cities.
TUR.story: Manzikert is Byzantium’s Asian undoing — the battle that turns Anatolia into Turkey’s future.

RUS.name: Vladimir–Suzdal / Novgorod
RUS.summary: Successor Rus’ polities under steppe pressure.
RUS.conflicts: Mongol/Golden Horde suzerainty; Novgorod–Sweden/Teutonic clashes in the north.
RUS.leaders: Alexander Nevsky; Moscow’s early Daniilovichi rising under Horde oversight.
RUS.religion: Orthodoxy under Mongol census and tribute.
RUS.culture: Prince–Horde diplomacy; monastic north; icon tradition.
RUS.story: Nevsky’s victories over Swedes/Teutonic knights and his Horde pragmatism become Russia’s double lesson: resist the West, bargain with the East.

UKR.name: Galicia–Volhynia
UKR.conflicts: Mongol pressure; Polish and Hungarian intervention.
UKR.leaders: Galicia–Volhynia princes; later Lithuanian overlords as the century turns.
UKR.religion: Orthodoxy; Mongol political suzerainty after Kiev’s fall.
UKR.story: Kiev’s sack (1240) ends an era; western Rus’ principalities become the bridge to Lithuanian rule.

CHE.name: Swiss forest cantons
CHE.leaders: Cantonal elites; Habsburg bailiffs as antagonists in legend.
CHE.story: The Rütli oath of later chronicle is Switzerland’s invented founding picnic — the real glue is victory over knights.

NLD.name: Low Countries principalities
NLD.leaders: Counts of Holland/Flanders; prince-bishops; urban magistrates.
NLD.culture: Cloth towns; early polder management; trade fairs.
NLD.story: Flemish cloth and communal power make the Low Countries rich before they are a country.

periods.label: Late Medieval
periods.narrative: The later Middle Ages open under the shadow of the Black Death (from 1347) and close toward gunpowder states and Renaissance courts. England and France bleed through the Hundred Years’ War; the Avignon papacy and Schism fracture Latin Christendom’s prestige; Burgundy flowers as a princely superpower; Iberian crowns push Granada; the Ottomans cross into Europe and crush Serbian and Byzantine power toward 1453; Poland and Lithuania join in personal union against the Teutonic Order and the steppe; Muscovy gathers Russian lands after the Golden Horde’s weakening. Culture: Gothic perpendicular and Flamboyant, vernacular literature (Chaucer, Dante’s afterlife, chivalric orders), and intensified devotional religion. Genetics: plague kills on a vast scale but does not invent new deep components — regional continua persist with mobility along war and trade.
periods.culturesNote: Hundred Years’ War realms; Burgundy; Crown of Aragon & Castile; Holy Roman mosaic; Jagiellon Poland–Lithuania; Ottoman Rumelia; Muscovy; Italian city-states.

iberia.description: Castile and Aragon (with Catalonia and Valencia) dominate Christian Iberia; Portugal is an Atlantic kingdom; Nasrid Granada survives as Islam’s last Iberian foothold under tribute and raid. Courtly culture mixes crusading ideology with Mediterranean commerce. Jewish and Muslim minorities remain crucial — and increasingly precarious — to urban economies. Ancestry is medieval Iberian continua with North African and earlier layers; politics is dynastic union building toward the Catholic Monarchs.
iberia.languages: Castilian, Portuguese, Catalan, etc.; Andalusi Arabic; Basque; Latin/Hebrew in domains
iberia.linguisticNote: Romance victory narrative with lasting Arabic loanwords and toponyms.
iberia.ancestryNote: Shifting clines from medieval contact; post-conquest homogenization incomplete.

britain.description: Plantagenet and then Lancastrian England fights for the French crown while Welsh revolt (Owain Glyndŵr) and Scottish wars flare. The Black Death empties manors and raises labor’s price; vernacular English (Chaucer) claims literary prestige beside French and Latin. Ireland remains a patchwork of English pale and Gaelic lordships. Genetics: plague mortality and mobility, not a new ancestral strand — continuity from high medieval Britain with aristocratic French ties.
britain.languages: Middle English; Anglo-Norman French; Welsh/Gaelic/Scots/etc.; Latin
britain.linguisticNote: Trilingual elite culture; English re-emerges as state language later.
britain.ancestryNote: Elite Norman layer; majority continuity from early medieval England.

france.description: Valois France fractures under English occupation, civil war (Armagnac–Burgundian), and Jacquerie social revolt, then slowly reconsolidates with gunpowder, taxes, and Joan of Arc’s mythic campaign. Burgundy’s dukes build a glittering state from Flanders to the Jura. Cathedrals, mystery plays, and royal sacral ideology define culture. Demography rebounds unevenly after plague on a Frankish–medieval French gene pool.
france.languages: Old/Middle French; Occitan; Breton; Basque edge; Latin
france.linguisticNote: Langue d’oïl vs oc is a major internal linguistic divide.
france.ancestryNote: Medieval France continuity; north/south structure persists.

central.description: The Holy Roman Empire is elective and plural: Luxemburg and early Habsburg emperors, Bohemian crown lands heading toward Hussite revolution, Swiss confederate victories, Teutonic Order vs Poland–Lithuania (Grünwald/Tannenberg 1410). German towns of the Hansa knit the Baltic. Latin and German law, Gothic art, and university theology (Prague, Vienna) shape elite culture. Ancestry: central European medieval continua.
central.languages: Middle High German; Czech/Polish/etc.; Italian vernaculars; Latin; Hungarian in the basin
central.linguisticNote: Empire ≠ one language; Latin and German as linking codes.
central.ancestryNote: German–Slavic contact zones show admixture; alpine/italian lands differ.

scandinavia.description: The Kalmar Union (from 1397) binds Denmark, Norway, and Sweden under one monarch in theory, with Swedish resistance never far away. Hanseatic merchants dominate Bergen and Baltic trade; Norwegian royal power wanes. Christianity is firmly Latin; vernacular laws and sagas persist in manuscript. Genetics track Nordic medieval populations — union is political, not a population replacement.
scandinavia.linguisticNote: From Old Norse relative unity to separate medieval standards.
scandinavia.ancestryNote: Continuous with Viking Age Nordic ternary; Christian medieval kingdoms are political-cultural, not a new genetic pulse.

italy.description: Visconti Milan, republican Florence, papal states, Naples, and maritime Venice/Genoa invent Renaissance patronage even before 1400’s end — humanism, vernacular epic, and mercenary condottieri. The south remains an Angevin then Aragonese prize. Urban density and plague shape demography; ancestry is Italian medieval continua with eastern Mediterranean trade contacts.
italy.languages: Italian dialects/volgare; Latin; Greek remnants in south
italy.linguisticNote: Dante’s era crystallizes literary Italian on a dialect continuum.
italy.ancestryNote: Ports cosmopolitan; hinterlands more local medieval Italian.

balkans.description: Serbian power peaks then falters (Kosovo 1389 in memory and politics); Bulgaria fragments; Byzantium is a rump around Constantinople; Ottoman beys and sultans take Gallipoli, Adrianople, and push north. Orthodox churches keep Slavic and Greek literacy under rising Islamic rule. This is conquest and conversion pressure on Balkan medieval ancestries — a political–religious transformation with gene flow along armies and slave routes, not a Mesolithic reset.
balkans.languageFamily: South Slavic + Greek + Albanian (emerging in record)
balkans.languages: Serbian/Bulgarian/etc.; Greek; Albanian; Romance islands; Latin in Catholic zones
balkans.linguisticNote: Medieval Balkan multilingualism before Ottoman overlay.
balkans.ancestryNote: Microregional mosaics; schematic continuity with early medieval Balkans.

eastern.culture: Rus’ principalities under Golden Horde pressure
eastern.description: The Golden Horde’s grip loosens; Moscow’s princes collect lands ‘of Rus’’ while Lithuania rules vast Ruthenian Orthodox populations under a pagan-then-Catholic elite. Jogaila’s union with Poland (1386) creates a dual realm facing Teutonic and Muscovite rivals. Steppe politics still matter; deep genetics remain eastern European continua with Turkic–Mongol elite layers.
eastern.languages: Old East Slavic varieties; Turkic; Mongol administration languages
eastern.linguisticNote: Court multilingualism over East Slavic countryside.
eastern.ancestryNote: Medieval East Slavic base + variable steppe/Mongol-era input.

periods.linguistics: Middle English rising in state use; Middle French; Early New High German; Italian vernaculars vs Latin; Castilian/Catalan/Portuguese; Church Slavonic & Ruthenian; Ottoman Turkish administration over Greek/Slavic/Albanian speakers.

GBR.name: Kingdom of England (Hundred Years’ War)
GBR.summary: English kings claim the French crown; longbow armies win Crécy and Agincourt; domestic politics slide toward the Wars of the Roses.
GBR.conflicts: Hundred Years’ War vs France; Scottish wars; Owain Glyndŵr’s Welsh revolt; later York–Lancaster civil war.
GBR.leaders: Edward III; the Black Prince; Richard II; Henry IV; Henry V; Henry VI.
GBR.religion: Latin Christianity under strain of papal Schism; Lollard dissent around Wycliffe’s Bible.
GBR.culture: Chaucer’s English; chivalric orders (Garter); perpendicular Gothic; growing parliamentary bargaining.
GBR.story: Agincourt (1415) becomes England’s mud-and-longbow miracle story — a outnumbered army’s victory that Tudor memory later wraps in nation-myth, even as the French war is eventually lost.

IRL.name: Lordship of Ireland & Gaelic polities
IRL.summary: English royal lordship holds a pale around Dublin while Gaelic and gaelicized Anglo-Irish lords dominate much of the island.
IRL.conflicts: Bruce invasion memory; local succession wars; crown neglect during French campaigns.
IRL.leaders: English lieutenants; great earls (Ormond, Desmond, Kildare rising); Gaelic kings of Tyrone/Thomond etc.
IRL.religion: Latin Christian; distinctive Gaelic church customs under reforming pressure.
IRL.culture: Bardic poetry; Brehon law zones; hybrid marcher culture.
IRL.story: Ireland’s late medieval story is unfinished conquest — enough English law to claim the island, not enough state to hold it.

FRA.name: Valois France & Burgundy
FRA.summary: France nearly disintegrates under English invasion and civil war, then reconquers with artillery, taxes, and Joan’s charismatic campaign.
FRA.conflicts: Hundred Years’ War; Armagnac–Burgundian feud; urban and peasant revolts.
FRA.leaders: Charles V; Charles VI; Charles VII; Joan of Arc; Philip the Good of Burgundy.
FRA.religion: Catholic kingdom; Gallican tensions with papacy; popular saint-cult around Joan.
FRA.culture: Flamboyant Gothic; courtly romance; emerging royal standing army.
FRA.story: Joan of Arc — peasant visionary who lifts the siege of Orléans and crowns Charles VII — is burned by the English then rehabilitated; France’s sacred rescue narrative.

DEU.name: Holy Roman Empire (late medieval)
DEU.summary: Elective emperors, imperial cities, and princely territories; Golden Bull order; Hussite wars shake Bohemia.
DEU.conflicts: Hussite crusades; Swiss victories vs Habsburgs; princely feuds; Ottoman pressure on the southeast later.
DEU.leaders: Charles IV; Wenceslaus; Sigismund; early Habsburgs (Albert II, Frederick III).
DEU.religion: Catholic mainstream; Hussite reform in Bohemia (Utraquists/Taborites); conciliar movement.
DEU.culture: Hansa trade; Gothic town halls; universities; vernacular German mysticism.
DEU.story: Jan Hus’s burning at Constance (1415) ignites Bohemia — a proto-Reformation of communion in both kinds, wagon-fort war, and Czech vernacular faith.

CZE.name: Lands of the Bohemian Crown
CZE.summary: Luxemburg emperors make Prague a capital of empire; Hussite revolution then reshapes Bohemian politics and confession.
CZE.conflicts: Hussite wars vs crusading Europe; internal Utraquist–Catholic settlement struggles.
CZE.leaders: Charles IV; Wenceslaus IV; Jan Hus; Jan Žižka; George of Poděbrady (later).
CZE.religion: Hussitism as national-religious movement inside/against Latin Christendom.
CZE.culture: Czech vernacular liturgy and song; Prague university; Gothic St Vitus.
CZE.story: Žižka’s blind generalship and wagon forts become Czech martial legend — peasants and townsmen beating knightly crusades.

POL.name: Kingdom of Poland (Jagiellon union)
POL.summary: Jogaila’s marriage union with Lithuania creates a dual power that breaks Teutonic expansion at Grünwald (1410).
POL.conflicts: Teutonic wars; Muscovite and Tatar frontiers via Lithuania; noble liberty rising.
POL.leaders: Władysław II Jagiełło; Vytautas the Great; later Jagiellon kings.
POL.religion: Catholic Poland with vast Orthodox Ruthenian populations under Lithuanian rule; pagan Lithuania’s conversion.
POL.culture: Latin and Ruthenian chanceries; knightly culture; growing szlachta identity.
POL.story: Grünwald/Tannenberg — a multinational Polish–Lithuanian–Ruthenian victory over the Teutonic Order — becomes Central Europe’s great anti-crusader epic.

LTU.name: Grand Duchy of Lithuania
LTU.summary: Europe’s last great pagan polity converts via Polish union yet rules mostly Orthodox Ruthenian lands from Vilnius.
LTU.conflicts: Teutonic crusades; rivalry and cooperation with Muscovy; Tatar alliances/wars.
LTU.religion: Catholic conversion of the elite; Orthodox majority in Ruthenian lands; residual pagan memory.
LTU.culture: Multiethnic duchy; Lithuanian dynasty over Slavic law codes; forest-and-steppe geopolitics.
LTU.story: Vytautas at the height of his power almost builds a Lithuanian empire from Baltic to Black Sea — a briefly plausible alternate Eastern Europe.

DNK.name: Kalmar Union (Danish center)
DNK.summary: Margaret I’s architecture unites Denmark, Norway, and Sweden under one monarch — Danish-led in practice.
DNK.conflicts: Swedish rebellions; Hanseatic wars; Norwegian dependency.
DNK.leaders: Margaret I; Eric of Pomerania; later Christian I.
DNK.religion: Latin Christian monarchies under Roman obedience.
DNK.culture: Baltic trade; royal castles; German merchant influence in towns.
DNK.story: Margaret I — ‘lady king’ of the North — engineers Scandinavia’s only durable medieval union, remembered as both peace project and Danish domination.

SWE.name: Sweden under / against Kalmar
SWE.summary: Swedish councils accept union then repeatedly rebel; Sture party later champions autonomy.
SWE.conflicts: Danish royal power; Hanseatic Stockholm politics; Finnish eastern frontier vs Novgorod/Muscovy.
SWE.leaders: Swedish regents (Sture line later); Engelbrekt’s revolt memory (1430s).
SWE.culture: Mining (Bergslagen); freeholding farmers; national chronicle beginnings.
SWE.story: Engelbrekt’s uprising becomes Sweden’s folk-hero revolt against union taxes and foreign bailiffs — a rehearsal of Vasa independence.

NOR.name: Norway in the Kalmar Union
NOR.summary: Norwegian royalty fades; the kingdom is the weaker partner under Danish monarchs and Hanseatic Bergen.
NOR.conflicts: Hansa dominance; black-death demographic shock earlier; loss of Atlantic vigor.
NOR.religion: Catholic archbishopric of Nidaros still prestigious.
NOR.culture: Saga manuscript culture persists; stockfish trade.
NOR.story: Norway’s late medieval arc is quiet tragedy: from independent sea kingdom to junior union partner — reversed only centuries later.

ESP.name: Castile & Aragon; Nasrid Granada
ESP.summary: Trastámara dynasties rule Castile and Aragon; Granada survives as a tributary Islamic emirate.
ESP.conflicts: Civil wars in Castile; Mediterranean expansion of Aragon (Sicily, Sardinia, Naples ambitions); frontier war with Granada.
ESP.leaders: John I / Henry III of Castile; Ferdinand I of Aragon; Yusuf/Nasrid emirs.
ESP.religion: Catholic majorities; Jewish communities under rising pressure; Islam in Granada.
ESP.culture: Alhambra’s late flowering; Castilian chivalric chronicle; Catalan commercial empire.
ESP.story: The Alhambra’s lyric courts exist beside a shrinking Islamic polity — beauty as the last act before 1492’s conquest.

PRT.name: Kingdom of Portugal (Aviz)
PRT.summary: After the 1385 crisis, Aviz kings secure independence from Castile and look toward Africa (Ceuta 1415).
PRT.conflicts: Castilian claims; Moroccan raids; Atlantic exploration beginnings under Henry the Navigator’s generation.
PRT.leaders: John I; Prince Henry the Navigator; Duarte.
PRT.culture: Atlantic seamanship; Gothic Batalha monastery as dynasty monument.
PRT.story: Aljubarrota (1385) saves Portuguese independence; Ceuta opens the African door that becomes the Age of Discovery.

ITA.name: Italian regional states
ITA.summary: Milan, Florence, Venice, the Papacy, and Naples balance in the ‘Italic League’ pattern — brilliant, fragile, mercenary.
ITA.conflicts: Condottieri wars; Ottoman naval pressure on Venice; Angevin/Aragonese fight for Naples.
ITA.leaders: Gian Galeazzo Visconti; Cosimo de’ Medici (rising); Venetian doges; rival popes in Schism’s wake.
ITA.culture: Early humanism; Dante/Petrarch/Boccaccio’s legacy; civic patronage.
ITA.story: Italian cities invent Renaissance modernity while failing to invent a durable Italian state — culture without unification.

GRC.name: Byzantine rump & Latin leftovers → Ottoman conquest
GRC.summary: Constantinople’s empire is a shadow waiting for 1453; Frankish and Venetian remnants linger in islands and ports.
GRC.conflicts: Ottoman siege pressure; civil wars; Western union diplomacy (Florence 1439) that divides Orthodox opinion.
GRC.leaders: Manuel II; John VIII; Constantine XI (mid-century); Ottoman Murad II / Mehmed II.
GRC.religion: Orthodoxy under existential threat; bitter debate over union with Rome.
GRC.culture: Late Byzantine scholarship fleeing westward; monastic Hesychasm.
GRC.story: The fall of Constantinople (1453) — Mehmed’s cannon vs Constantine XI’s last stand — ends the Roman imperial story in Greek dress and becomes Christendom’s great lament.

SRB.name: Serbian lands after the empire
SRB.summary: Post-Dušan fragmentation; Kosovo battle memory; eventual Ottoman subjugation of Serbian despots.
SRB.conflicts: Ottoman advance; Hungarian alliances; internal magnate splits.
SRB.leaders: Prince Lazar (memory of Kosovo); despot Stefan Lazarević; later Durad Branković.
SRB.religion: Serbian Orthodoxy as identity under pressure.
SRB.culture: Epic poetry cycle of Kosovo; monastery patronage (Morava school).
SRB.story: Kosovo Polje (1389) becomes Serbia’s central martyrdom epic — historically messy, culturally absolute.

BGR.name: Bulgarian lands under Ottoman conquest
BGR.summary: Second Bulgarian Empire’s fragments fall to Ottoman campaigns in the late 14th century.
BGR.conflicts: Ottoman conquest; resistance and boyar accommodation.
BGR.leaders: Last Shishmanids; local notables under early Ottoman rule.
BGR.religion: Orthodoxy under the millet-to-be; Islamization limited at first.
BGR.culture: Tarnovo literary memory; then Ottoman provincial order.
BGR.story: The end of medieval Bulgarian statehood is told as nightfall before centuries of foreign rule — a national narrative forged later, rooted in real conquest.

RUS.name: Grand Principality of Moscow
RUS.summary: Moscow ‘gathers the Russian lands,’ contests Novgorod, and maneuvers between Horde overlords and Lithuania.
RUS.conflicts: Wars with Novgorod, Tver, Lithuania; tribute and rebellion vs the Horde (Ugra 1480 still ahead as symbolic end).
RUS.leaders: Dmitry Donskoy; Vasily I; Vasily II; Ivan III (later in century).
RUS.religion: Orthodox metropolitanate shifting toward Moscow; monastic colonization of the north.
RUS.culture: Icon painting; chronicle writing; fortress kremlins.
RUS.story: Kulikovo (1380) — Dmitry’s victory over a Horde commander — becomes Russia’s first great liberation myth, even though Horde power returns afterward.

UKR.name: Ruthenian lands under Lithuania
UKR.summary: Former Kievan territories largely ruled from Vilnius; Orthodox boyars under Lithuanian/Polish union politics.
UKR.conflicts: Tatar raids; Muscovite claims on ‘Rus’ heritage’; local princely remnants.
UKR.leaders: Lithuanian grand dukes; Ruthenian princes (Ostroski later prominence).
UKR.religion: Orthodoxy majority; Catholic elite conversion pressures after Krewo/Horodło.
UKR.culture: Ruthenian chancery language; fortress towns; steppe border life.
UKR.story: Who inherits Kiev’s legacy — Moscow or Lithuania’s Rus’ — is the ideological war of the late medieval east.

HUN.name: Kingdom of Hungary (Anjou → Luxemburg/Habsburg claims)
HUN.summary: A major Central European kingdom facing Ottoman pressure on its southern frontier after Serbian collapse.
HUN.conflicts: Ottoman raids; succession crises; baron leagues.
HUN.leaders: Louis I the Great (memory); Sigismund of Luxemburg; later Hunyadi (mid-century).
HUN.religion: Catholic realm with Orthodox minorities in the south/east.
HUN.culture: Chivalric court; Gothic Buda; multiethnic nobility.
HUN.story: Hungary casts itself as Christendom’s shield; the 15th-century Hunyadi wars turn that claim into cannon-smoke reality.

NLD.name: Burgundian Netherlands
NLD.summary: Flanders and the Low Countries under Burgundian dukes become Europe’s richest urban–textile zone.
NLD.conflicts: Urban revolts; French/English war entanglement; later Habsburg inheritance.
NLD.leaders: Philip the Bold; John the Fearless; Philip the Good.
NLD.religion: Dense parish Catholicism; early reform currents still underground.
NLD.culture: Early Netherlandish painting; cloth towns; pragmatic urban liberties.
NLD.story: Burgundy’s court — Order of the Golden Fleece, dazzling chronicles — makes the Low Countries a capital of European splendor without being a ‘nation’ yet.

CHE.name: Swiss Confederation
CHE.summary: Alpine cantons defeat Habsburg knights and become a fact of European military life.
CHE.conflicts: Habsburg wars; Burgundian wars (later 15th c.); internal canton politics.
CHE.leaders: Cantonal elites; legendary William Tell as later national myth layered on real battles (Morgarten, Sempach).
CHE.religion: Catholic; local saints and fierce communal autonomy.
CHE.story: Sempach and Morgarten are Switzerland’s founding battle-stories: infantry and terrain beating aristocratic cavalry.

AUT.name: Habsburg Austrian lands
AUT.summary: Habsburgs consolidate Alpine duchies and begin their long game for empire and Burgundian inheritance.
AUT.conflicts: Swiss losses; Bohemian/Hungarian dynastic contests; Ottoman shadow later.
AUT.leaders: Rudolf IV (memory); Albert II; Frederick III (‘AEIOU’).
AUT.culture: Vienna as rising residence; dynastic marriage strategy elevated to art.
AUT.story: Frederick III’s cryptic AEIOU and Maximilian’s later Burgundian wedding embody Habsburg doctrine: marry, inherit, outlast.

TUR.name: Ottoman Sultanate in Europe
TUR.summary: From Rumelian bases the Ottomans become a European great power before taking Constantinople.
TUR.conflicts: Wars with Serbia, Bulgaria, Hungary, Byzantium, Venice; Anatolian rivals.
TUR.leaders: Bayezid I; Mehmed I; Murad II; Mehmed II.
TUR.religion: Sunni Islam as state; dhimmi system for Christians and Jews.
TUR.culture: Ghazi warrior ethos evolving into imperial bureaucracy; endowment (waqf) cities.
TUR.story: The lightning rise from frontier beylik to breaker of Constantinople reorders Europe’s mental map — Islam as a Central European neighbor.

periods.label: Reformation & Renaissance
periods.narrative: By the mid-16th century Europe is split by confession and stitched by dynastic empire. Luther, Calvin, and the Catholic Council of Trent redraw belief; print multiplies argument; Habsburgs claim Spain’s global monarchy and the imperial title; Valois then early Bourbon France fights Habsburg encirclement and its own Wars of Religion; Tudor England breaks with Rome; the Ottomans under Süleyman dominate the Balkans and menace Vienna; Ivan IV’s Muscovy becomes an autocratic Orthodox empire; the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth is a noble republic of many faiths; Dutch revolt against Philip II is beginning. Overseas Iberian empires pull silver and souls into European politics. Genetics still sit on medieval continua — conversion and empire move people, but WHG–EEF–steppe deep structure remains.
periods.culturesNote: Habsburg Spain & Austria; Valois France; Tudor England; Lutheran North; Ottoman Rumelia; Muscovy; PLC; Italian Mannerism; Portuguese & Spanish oceans.

iberia.description: Spain under Charles V and Philip II is a composite global monarchy: Castile’s silver fleets, Aragon’s Mediterranean inheritance, Portuguese dynastic entanglement (Iberian Union from 1580). Catholic reform, Inquisition, and expulsion/forced conversion of Muslims and Jews reshape society after Granada’s fall (1492). Culture: Golden Age letters and severe Habsburg piety. Ancestry: medieval Iberia plus Atlantic/imperial contacts — not a new ternary corner.
iberia.linguisticNote: Castilian and Portuguese become world languages from these metropoles.
iberia.ancestryNote: Early modern Iberia ≈ late medieval clines + port diversity; empires transform the Americas more than Iberian deep ancestry.

britain.description: Tudor England — Henry VIII’s break with Rome, Edwardine Protestantism, Mary’s Catholic restoration, Elizabeth’s settlement — invents a national church and fights Spain’s Armada decade. Scotland’s Reformation (Knox) and Ireland’s Tudor conquest wars create three different confessional trajectories on closely related islands. Print, Bible English, and Renaissance humanism redefine elite culture on a late medieval English gene pool.
britain.languages: Early Modern English; Welsh, Irish, Scottish Gaelic, Scots…
britain.ancestryNote: Early modern continuity with medieval Britain; later empire-era migration still limited vs 20th c.

france.description: Valois France oscillates between Italian Wars glory and catastrophic Wars of Religion (Catholic League vs Huguenots) after the 1560s. Royal sacral power meets Calvinist nobles and Parisian radicalism; St Bartholomew’s Day becomes a European trauma story. Art and chateaux of the Renaissance coexist with confessional massacre. Demography is French medieval continuity under extreme political violence.
france.languages: Classical French standardizing; Occitan, Breton, Basque, German dialects, etc.
france.linguisticNote: State language policy begins long pressure on regional langues.
france.ancestryNote: Regional deep structure under one polity label.

central.description: The Holy Roman Empire after the Peace of Augsburg (1555) legalizes cuius regio, eius religio for Lutheran and Catholic princes — a truce before the Thirty Years’ War. Habsburgs hold Austria, Bohemia, Hungary’s remnant against Ottomans; German towns print pamphlets; Swiss cantons host Zwingli/Calvin’s orbits. Culture: confessional schooling, vernacular Bible, and Mannerist courts. Ancestry: central European continua.
central.languages: Early New High German; Czech; Hungarian; Polish; Yiddish; Italian; etc.
central.ancestryNote: Early modern Mitteleuropa continuity + war displacements.

scandinavia.description: Denmark–Norway and Sweden become Lutheran monarchies; Gustav Vasa’s Sweden breaks Kalmar dependency and builds a fiscal-military state. Church lands fund kings; vernacular Bibles standardize speech. Baltic rivalry with Poland and Muscovy replaces union politics. Genetics: Nordic continuity through Reformation institutional change.
scandinavia.linguisticNote: Bible translations and chanceries fix standards.
scandinavia.ancestryNote: Continuous with medieval Norden; great-power wars move armies more than they reset homeland ancestry.

italy.description: Italian wars make the peninsula a Habsburg–Valois battlefield; Spanish Naples and Milan, papal Rome’s Counter-Reformation, Venetian maritime republic, and Tuscan ducal courts define politics. High Renaissance and Mannerism radiate artistic norms across Europe even as political independence wanes. Ancestry: Italian urban–rural medieval mixes with Spanish/Imperial elite overlays.
italy.linguisticNote: Literary Italian without political unity yet.
italy.ancestryNote: Stable north–south structure; ports remain diverse.

balkans.description: Ottoman rule is entrenched across much of the Balkans: timar cavalry, millet confessional autonomy for Orthodox Christians and Jews, Islamization uneven by region (stronger in parts of Bosnia, Albania). Hungarian kingdom is split among Habsburg, Ottoman, and Transylvanian pieces after Mohács (1526). Culture: Orthodox monasteries, Sufi orders, and frontier epics. Genetics: Balkan continua plus Ottoman-era mobility.
balkans.ancestryNote: Elevated “other” as uncertainty band for Ottoman-era inputs; microregional.
balkans.languages: Ottoman Turkish; South Slavic; Greek; Albanian; Romance (e.g. Vlach); others
balkans.linguisticNote: Imperial Turkish + local vernaculars; religion often structures language domains.

eastern.description: Ivan IV (‘the Terrible’) crowns a tsardom, conquers Kazan and Astrakhan, and opens a violent chapter of autocracy and expansion. The Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth (Union of Lublin 1569) is a vast elective noble republic tolerating multiple faiths at elite level while binding Ruthenian lands. Cossack frontiers and Tatar raids frame the steppe edge. Deep ancestry remains eastern European; the novelty is tsarist and Commonwealth institutions.
eastern.languages: Polish; Ruthenian/Ukrainian; Russian; Lithuanian; Yiddish; German; Tatar…
eastern.linguisticNote: PLC nested multilingualism vs Russian imperial centralization later.
eastern.ancestryNote: Slavic-majority demography with Baltic, Finnic, Turkic, and other minorities.

periods.linguistics: Early Modern English; Middle/early modern French; Early New High German; Castilian imperial standard; Italian literary language; Polish & Ruthenian; Church Slavonic/Russian chancery; Ottoman Turkish; Latin still scholarly.

GBR.name: Tudor England (& Reformation Scotland)
GBR.summary: Henry VIII’s royal supremacy, Edward’s Protestant turn, Mary’s Catholic restoration, and Elizabeth’s settlement create a confessional rollercoaster; Scotland adopts a Calvinist kirk.
GBR.conflicts: Rough Wooing vs Scotland; Irish Tudor conquest wars; rivalry with Spain culminating in the Armada (1588).
GBR.leaders: Henry VIII; Edward VI; Mary I; Elizabeth I; Mary Queen of Scots; John Knox.
GBR.religion: Church of England via statute; Catholic underground; Puritan pressure; Scottish Presbyterianism.
GBR.culture: Vernacular Bible and Book of Common Prayer; emerging public theatre (Elizabethan); humanist schools.
GBR.story: The Armada — storm, fireships, and propaganda — becomes Protestant England’s deliverance myth; Mary Queen of Scots’ scaffold is the tragic counter-story of Catholic royalty.

IRL.name: Tudor Ireland
IRL.summary: Surrender-and-regrant and plantation beginnings aim to anglicize Gaelic lordships; resistance culminates later in the Nine Years’ War.
IRL.conflicts: Desmond rebellions; Shane O’Neill; crown vs Gaelic alliances.
IRL.leaders: Tudor deputies; Shane O’Neill; earls of Desmond; Hugh O’Neill (later).
IRL.religion: Catholic population under a Protestant state church newly claimed.
IRL.culture: Gaelic learned orders under pressure; Pale Englishness vs Gaelic polarity hardening.
IRL.story: Ireland becomes England’s first long colonial laboratory — Reformation plus conquest, with consequences lasting centuries.

FRA.name: Valois France in the Wars of Religion
FRA.summary: Italian Wars prestige collapses into Catholic–Huguenot civil wars; monarchy nearly dissolves before Bourbon recovery.
FRA.conflicts: Habsburg wars; eight Wars of Religion; St Bartholomew’s Massacre; Catholic League vs Henry of Navarre.
FRA.leaders: Francis I; Henry II; Catherine de’ Medici; Henry III; Henry IV (Navarre).
FRA.religion: Catholic majority; Calvinist Huguenot minority with noble leadership; politiques seeking peace.
FRA.culture: Renaissance chateaux; Rabelais/Montaigne; militant confessional print.
FRA.story: St Bartholomew’s Day (1572) — wedding turned massacre — scars Europe; Henry IV’s later ‘Paris is worth a mass’ pragmatism ends the nightmare (Edict of Nantes 1598).

ESP.name: Spanish Habsburg world monarchy
ESP.summary: Charles V and Philip II rule Spain, much of Italy, the Low Countries, and American silver — Catholic champion and bankrupt giant.
ESP.conflicts: Dutch Revolt; Ottoman Mediterranean war (Lepanto 1571); English war; French Habsburg rivalry; Morisco revolt.
ESP.leaders: Charles V; Philip II; Duke of Alba; Don John of Austria.
ESP.culture: Golden Age literature beginnings; Escorial austerity; global bureaucracy.
ESP.story: Lepanto is sung as Christian naval triumph; the Dutch Revolt and Armada failure show the limits of Spanish universal monarchy.

PRT.name: Portuguese Empire (& Iberian Union ahead)
PRT.summary: Portugal’s Asian and Brazilian routes still enrich the crown; dynastic crisis will hand the realm to Philip II in 1580.
PRT.conflicts: Ottoman and local Asian rivals; French/English interlopers; Moroccan disaster at Alcácer Quibir (1578).
PRT.leaders: John III; Sebastian I; Cardinal-King Henry.
PRT.religion: Catholic missionary orders (Jesuits) as empire’s soft power.
PRT.culture: Camões’ epic of discovery (Os Lusíadas, 1572); Atlantic Creole ports.
PRT.story: Sebastian’s death in Morocco becomes the sebastianismo myth — a lost king who will return — while Spain absorbs the Portuguese crown.

DEU.name: Confessional Holy Roman Empire
DEU.summary: Augsburg’s peace freezes Lutheran and Catholic princely choice; Calvinists remain legally awkward; print culture never freezes.
DEU.conflicts: Princely rivalries; Ottoman wars on Habsburg borders; prelude tensions to 1618.
DEU.leaders: Charles V (earlier); Ferdinand I; Lutheran princes (Saxon/Electorates); Protestant Union / Catholic League seeds.
DEU.religion: Lutheran / Catholic official duality; Calvinist expansion; Anabaptist memory of persecution.
DEU.culture: Vernacular Bible; Lutheran chorale; university confessionalization; Dürer’s legacy into Mannerism.
DEU.story: Luther at Worms (‘here I stand’ in later wording) remains the origin scene; Augsburg 1555 is the exhausted compromise that only postpones a continental war.

NLD.name: Habsburg Netherlands → Dutch Revolt
NLD.summary: Rich urban provinces revolt against Philip II’s taxes, troops, and heresy laws; a republic is being born.
NLD.conflicts: Iconoclastic Fury; Alba’s Council of Blood; siege warfare; William of Orange’s leadership.
NLD.leaders: William the Silent; Philip II’s governors (Alba, Requesens, Parma); Beggars (Geuzen).
NLD.religion: Calvinist revolt core; large Catholic populations; radical tolerance experiments in places.
NLD.culture: Early capitalist trade; print and pamphlets; art before the Golden Age bloom.
NLD.story: The Sea Beggars’ capture of Brielle (1572) is the revolt’s spark-story — a ragged naval rebel act that unravels Spanish authority in Holland and Zeeland.

CHE.name: Swiss Confederation (Reformation)
CHE.summary: Zwingli’s Zurich and Calvin’s Geneva make Switzerland a laboratory of Reformed religion beside Catholic cantons.
CHE.conflicts: Kappel wars between confessions; mercenary export continues.
CHE.leaders: Ulrich Zwingli; John Calvin; Catholic Waldstätten elites.
CHE.religion: Reformed vs Catholic cantonal split — a miniature Europe.
CHE.culture: Disciplined consistory religion; citizen-soldier myth; printing.
CHE.story: Calvin’s Geneva — refuge for exiles and exporter of pastors — punches far above its Alpine weight in Atlantic Protestantism.

ITA.name: Italian states under Habsburg hegemony
ITA.summary: Spanish Milan and Naples, papal Counter-Reformation Rome, Tuscan dukes, and Venice define a politically subordinated, culturally radiant Italy.
ITA.conflicts: French residual wars; Ottoman–Venetian sea war; heresy trials.
ITA.leaders: Cosimo I de’ Medici; papal reformers (Paul III →); Spanish viceroys; Venetian doges.
ITA.religion: Tridentine Catholicism; Index and Inquisition; Jewish ghettos formalized in places.
ITA.culture: Late Renaissance/Mannerism; early scientific circles; opera’s eve.
ITA.story: Rome rebrands as Caput Mundi of Catholic reform while Machiavelli’s earlier mirror of princes teaches Europe a colder politics than the popes prefer.

SWE.name: Vasa Sweden
SWE.summary: Gustav Vasa’s hereditary Lutheran monarchy breaks Kalmar and builds a resource state from church lands and copper.
SWE.conflicts: Danish wars; peasant risings (Dacke); Baltic competition with Russia/Poland.
SWE.leaders: Gustav Vasa; Eric XIV; John III.
SWE.religion: Lutheran state church; residual Catholic liturgy fights under John III.
SWE.culture: National chronicle; fortress modernisation; Finnish eastern marches.
SWE.story: Gustav’s rebellion against Kristian II (Stockholm Bloodbath memory) is Sweden’s independence epic — blood, tax, and Bible.

DNK.name: Denmark–Norway (Lutheran)
DNK.summary: Oldenburg kings run a Lutheran dual monarchy controlling the Øresund toll — Europe’s choke point to the Baltic.
DNK.conflicts: Swedish independence wars; Baltic rivalry; Norwegian incorporation.
DNK.religion: Lutheran Reformation imposed after civil war (Count’s Feud).
DNK.culture: Sound Toll wealth; Renaissance Kronborg; Norwegian dependency.
DNK.story: Whoever holds the Sound Toll taxes half of northern Europe’s grain and naval stores — Denmark’s geopolitical superpower trick.

NOR.name: Norway under Denmark
NOR.summary: A kingdom without its own resident dynasty; Reformation arrives via Copenhagen.
NOR.conflicts: Danish governors; trade under Hansa then Danish control.
NOR.culture: Continuing vernacular life; loss of archbishopric independence.
NOR.story: Norway’s Reformation is an email from Copenhagen — institutional change without a local Luther.

POL.name: Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth
POL.summary: Union of Lublin (1569) creates a vast elective republic of nobles, multiethnic and (at elite level) multi-confessional.
POL.conflicts: Muscovite wars; Baltic contests with Sweden; Ottoman/Tatar south; noble liberty vs royal power.
POL.leaders: Sigismund II Augustus; later Henry Valois / Stephen Báthory (election politics).
POL.religion: Catholic, Orthodox, Protestant, and Jewish communities under the Warsaw Confederation’s famous tolerance act (1573).
POL.culture: Szlachta golden liberty; Latin and Polish Renaissance; Ruthenian borders.
POL.story: The Commonwealth’s noble democracy — liberum ideas before the word — is Europe’s alternate modernity: huge, tolerant, and hard to mobilize.

LTU.name: Lithuania within the Commonwealth
LTU.summary: The Grand Duchy retains law and identity inside the Lublin union while sharing foreign policy and elective kingship with Poland.
LTU.conflicts: Muscovite pressure; internal integration with Polish institutions.
LTU.leaders: Sigismund Augustus as both; Lithuanian magnate families (Radziwiłł).
LTU.religion: Catholicizing elites; Orthodox and Protestant magnates; Jewish towns.
LTU.story: Lublin is both marriage and partial erasure — Lithuanian statehood persists in law while European maps increasingly say ‘Poland.’

RUS.name: Tsardom of Russia (Ivan IV)
RUS.summary: Ivan IV crowns himself tsar, conquers Muslim khanates on the Volga, then unleashes the Oprichnina’s terror.
RUS.conflicts: Livonian War vs Poland/Sweden; Crimean Tatar sack of Moscow (1571); internal blood purge.
RUS.leaders: Ivan IV (‘the Terrible’); advisers then victims of the Oprichnina; Yermak’s Cossack Siberia beginnings.
RUS.religion: Orthodox autocracy; Moscow as ‘Third Rome’ ideology rising.
RUS.culture: Onion-dome votive architecture; chronicle and terror; eastward conquest.
RUS.story: Ivan’s killing of his own son (in later tradition) and the Oprichnina make him Europe’s archetype of sacred tyranny — expansion and self-devouring power.

UKR.name: Ukrainian lands: Commonwealth borderland
UKR.summary: Ruthenian provinces of the Commonwealth; Cossack militarized frontiers against Tatars and as royal/noble instruments.
UKR.conflicts: Tatar slave raids; magnate estates; emerging Cossack political identity (rebellions later in the 17th c.).
UKR.leaders: Wisniowiecki and other magnates; Cossack starshyna forming; Crimean khans as raid-neighbors.
UKR.religion: Orthodoxy under pressure of Catholic/Uniate projects (Brest 1596 just ahead/around this horizon).
UKR.culture: Steppe frontier epic; church brotherhoods; bilingual Polish–Ruthenian elite zone.
UKR.story: The Cossack — freeman warrior of the Dnieper cataracts — becomes Ukraine’s lasting social myth, born on this violent border.

HUN.name: Hungary divided (Ottoman / Habsburg / Transylvania)
HUN.summary: After Mohács, the medieval kingdom splits into Habsburg Royal Hungary, Ottoman central occupation, and the Principality of Transylvania.
HUN.conflicts: Ottoman–Habsburg wars; Transylvanian diplomacy between sultans and emperors.
HUN.leaders: Ferdinand I Habsburg; János Szapolyai’s line; Ottoman pashas of Buda; Transylvanian princes.
HUN.religion: Catholic Habsburg west; Protestant strength in Transylvania’s famous tolerance diet; Orthodox Romanians; Islam in Ottoman zones.
HUN.culture: Frontier fortress warfare; multi-confessional Transylvania as outlier.
HUN.story: Mohács (1526) — two hours that kill a king and shatter a kingdom — is Hungary’s national catastrophe date.

AUT.name: Austrian Habsburg core
AUT.summary: Vienna’s Habsburgs defend and administer the Danube frontier while claiming the imperial title and Spanish kinship.
AUT.conflicts: Ottoman sieges (1529 memory); German princely politics; Bohemian crown lands.
AUT.leaders: Ferdinand I; Maximilian II; Spanish kin Philip II.
AUT.religion: Catholic dynasty with temporarily tolerant Maximilian; Jesuit education rising.
AUT.story: The 1529 Ottoman siege of Vienna teaches Europe that the Turk can reach the heart of the Reich — fear as policy.

GRC.name: Ottoman Greece
GRC.summary: Greek lands under Ottoman provinces; Orthodox Patriarchate in Constantinople as millet head; islands partly Venetian.
GRC.conflicts: Venetian–Ottoman wars; local bandit/klepht beginnings; tax and conversion pressures.
GRC.leaders: Ecumenical Patriarchs; Ottoman governors; Venetian captains in the islands.
GRC.religion: Greek Orthodoxy under Islamic sovereignty; crypto-Christianity debates in places.
GRC.culture: Post-Byzantine painting; folk song; diaspora merchants.
GRC.story: The ‘secret school’ legend of keeping Greek letters alive under Ottoman rule is later nation-myth — literacy and liturgy did persist, unevenly, through church structures.

BGR.name: Ottoman Bulgaria
BGR.summary: Bulgarian lands as Ottoman provinces; Orthodox church life continues under the Patriarchate.
BGR.conflicts: Local uprisings occasional; integration into Ottoman fiscal systems.
BGR.leaders: Ottoman officials; Orthodox bishops; local çorbacı notables.
BGR.religion: Orthodoxy; gradual Islamization in some regions.
BGR.story: Bulgarian national revival is centuries away; this is the long Ottoman night of later historiography — daily life more continuous than the metaphor suggests.

SRB.name: Ottoman Serbia (& Habsburg fringe)
SRB.summary: Serbian lands largely Ottoman; patriarchate of Peć sometimes restored as communal focus; migrations north toward Habsburg lands begin in pulses.
SRB.conflicts: Ottoman–Habsburg wars; local knez autonomy pockets.
SRB.leaders: Ottoman pashas; Serbian patriarchs; hajduk outlaw-heroes in folk song.
SRB.religion: Southern Slavic Orthodoxy under millet structures.
SRB.story: The hajduk — outlaw resistance figure — becomes the folk counter-state when there is no Serbian kingdom on the map.

TUR.name: Ottoman imperial center
TUR.summary: Süleyman’s empire straddles three continents; Istanbul is a world capital of law, architecture, and war.
TUR.conflicts: Safavid wars; Habsburg frontier; Mediterranean rivalry with Spain/Venice; Indian Ocean contests with Portugal.
TUR.leaders: Süleyman the Magnificent; grand viziers (e.g. Rüstem, Sokollu); Hürrem Sultan in court politics.
TUR.religion: Sunni Islam (Hanafi law); protected Christian and Jewish millets; Sufi orders.
TUR.culture: Sinan’s mosques; kanun law beside sharia; multilingual palace.
TUR.story: Süleyman before Vienna and at Mohács makes the sultan Europe’s indispensable villain and diplomat — the ‘Magnificent’ as mirror to Charles V.

BEL.name: Southern Netherlands (Spanish)
BEL.summary: The Catholic southern provinces reconquered by Parma remain under Spanish Habsburgs as Antwerp’s golden age wanes.
BEL.conflicts: Dutch Revolt warfare; religious cleansing northward migration of Protestants.
BEL.leaders: Duke of Parma (Alexander Farnese); Spanish governors.
BEL.culture: Flemish painting still luminous; commercial shift toward Amsterdam.
BEL.story: Antwerp’s fall and Protestant exodus help invent Amsterdam’s boom — a tale of two Low Countries.

periods.label: Early Modern
periods.narrative: Print, Reformation, and composite monarchies: Spanish/Portuguese global empires, France, England→Britain, Habsburgs, Ottoman Europe, Poland–Lithuania, Sweden’s great-power age, rising Russia. Sovereignty and confession redraw maps; deep autosomal structure still echoes Neolithic and Bronze Age pulses, with Ottoman, imperial, and port-city admixture in specific corridors.
periods.culturesNote: Spanish & Portuguese empires, France, England/Britain, Habsburg Mitteleuropa, Ottoman Rumelia, PLC, Sweden, Muscovy/Russia.

iberia.description: Spanish Habsburgs preside over a global monarchy already feeling overstretch: Dutch war, Catalan and Portuguese revolts, literary Golden Age, and American silver. Portugal restores independence in 1640 after Iberian Union. Demography: plague, emigration to empire, and Morisco expulsions earlier reshape society on medieval Iberian ancestries.
iberia.linguisticNote: Castilian and Portuguese become world languages from these metropoles.
iberia.ancestryNote: Early modern Iberia ≈ late medieval clines + port diversity; empires transform the Americas more than Iberian deep ancestry.

britain.description: Union of Crowns (1603) joins Scotland and England under one monarch while Ireland’s conquest and plantation deepen. Civil war, regicide, republic, and Restoration rewrite the meaning of kingship; Navigation Acts and colonies pull the islands into Atlantic empire. Confessional conflict (Anglican, Puritan, Presbyterian, Catholic) is the political language of the century. Genetics: early modern British continua with Irish war demography and growing colonial entanglement — still the medieval ternary at depth.
britain.languages: Early Modern English; Welsh, Irish, Scottish Gaelic, Scots…
britain.ancestryNote: Early modern continuity with medieval Britain; later empire-era migration still limited vs 20th c.

france.description: From Henry IV’s reconstruction through Richelieu and toward Louis XIV, France invents fiscal-military absolutism, tames Huguenot military power, and enters the Thirty Years’ War as a great power. Classical French culture and Versailles politics (later in the century) radiate norms. Ancestry: French medieval continuity under state centralization and war mortality.
france.languages: Classical French standardizing; Occitan, Breton, Basque, German dialects, etc.
france.linguisticNote: State language policy begins long pressure on regional langues.
france.ancestryNote: Regional deep structure under one polity label.

central.description: The Thirty Years’ War guts the Holy Roman Empire; Westphalia (1648) legalizes confessional plurality and strengthens princes. Habsburgs refocus on Austria/Bohemia/Hungary and the Ottoman frontier; Brandenburg rises. Culture: baroque rebuilding on demographic ruin. Genetics: war losses and mobility without a new deep ancestral strand.
central.languages: Early New High German; Czech; Hungarian; Polish; Yiddish; Italian; etc.
central.ancestryNote: Early modern Mitteleuropa continuity + war displacements.

scandinavia.description: Sweden’s great-power century (Gustavus Adolphus to Charles XII’s eve) dominates the Baltic; Denmark–Norway defends the Sound; Finland is Sweden’s eastern wing. Lutheran orthodoxy and military conscription define society. Ancestry: Nordic continua under imperial Swedish extraction of men and copper.
scandinavia.linguisticNote: Bible translations and chanceries fix standards.
scandinavia.ancestryNote: Continuous with medieval Norden; great-power wars move armies more than they reset homeland ancestry.

italy.description: Spanish Habsburg hegemony over Milan and Naples; papal baroque Rome; Venetian twilight; Savoy’s slow rise. Galileo’s trial and baroque art make Italy Europe’s cultural exporter and political dependent. Ancestry: Italian early modern continua with Spanish elite overlays.
italy.linguisticNote: Literary Italian without political unity yet.
italy.ancestryNote: Stable north–south structure; ports remain diverse.

balkans.description: Ottoman rule remains the political frame for much of the Balkans; Habsburg–Ottoman wars pulse along the Military Frontier; Orthodox millets organize Christian life. Islamization varies by region. Genetics: Balkan continua plus frontier resettlements.
balkans.ancestryNote: Elevated “other” as uncertainty band for Ottoman-era inputs; microregional.
balkans.languages: Ottoman Turkish; South Slavic; Greek; Albanian; Romance (e.g. Vlach); others
balkans.linguisticNote: Imperial Turkish + local vernaculars; religion often structures language domains.

eastern.description: Russia exits the Time of Troubles into Romanov consolidation and begins to press Poland and Siberia; the Commonwealth enters the Deluge’s disasters; Cossack uprisings remake Ukraine’s politics. Deep ancestry unchanged in kind; the story is serfdom, autocracy, and noble republic in collision.
eastern.languages: Polish; Ruthenian/Ukrainian; Russian; Lithuanian; Yiddish; German; Tatar…
eastern.linguisticNote: PLC nested multilingualism vs Russian imperial centralization later.
eastern.ancestryNote: Slavic-majority demography with Baltic, Finnic, Turkic, and other minorities.

periods.linguistics: Standardizing national languages; Latin retreats from administration; Ottoman Turkish as imperial language in the Balkans; colonial Spanish/Portuguese/English/French radiate overseas.

ESP.name: Spanish Habsburg monarchy
ESP.conflicts: Dutch Revolt; wars with France/England; Ottoman Mediterranean war.
ESP.leaders: Philip III; Philip IV; Olivares; continuing Habsburg line.
ESP.story: Don Quixote (1605) laughs a tired empire into world literature while silver fleets and bankruptcies continue offstage.

PRT.name: Portuguese Empire
PRT.conflicts: Dutch conflicts overseas; Spanish dynastic entanglement.
PRT.leaders: Philip III of Spain during Iberian Union phases; Portuguese restoration leaders later (1640).
PRT.story: The 1640 restoration against Spain becomes Portugal’s second independence epic.

FRA.name: Kingdom of France
FRA.summary: Wars of Religion into Bourbon consolidation.
FRA.conflicts: Habsburg encirclement wars; later Thirty Years’ involvement.
FRA.leaders: Henry IV; Richelieu; Louis XIV (later flowering from mid-century).
FRA.religion: Edict of Nantes coexistence then later revocation trajectory; Catholic reform.
FRA.culture: Classical French taste forming; absolutist administration.
FRA.story: Richelieu’s state-within-the-state and the siege of La Rochelle dramatize the taming of armed faith for royal sovereignty.

GBR.name: England → Britain
GBR.conflicts: Anglo-Spanish war; Irish conquest; civil wars mid-century.
GBR.leaders: Elizabeth I (late); James VI & I; Charles I; Cromwell; William & Mary (long 17th-c. arc around the 1600 tick).
GBR.religion: Protestant settlements; Puritan revolution; Catholic minorities; Scottish kirk conflicts.
GBR.culture: Shakespearean stage; scientific circles toward the Royal Society; Atlantic colonization.
GBR.story: The Civil War and regicide of Charles I shock Europe — a king tried by his people — before Restoration and Glorious Revolution redefine monarchy.

NLD.name: Dutch Republic
NLD.conflicts: Eighty Years’ War; Anglo-Dutch wars; colonial rivalry.
NLD.leaders: Oldenbarnevelt; Maurice of Nassau; later Johan de Witt / William III arc.
NLD.religion: Public Calvinism with notable practical tolerance in cities.
NLD.culture: Dutch Golden Age art (Rembrandt, Vermeer); global VOC capitalism.
NLD.story: A republic of US merchants defeats Spain and paints light onto canvas — Europe’s miracle of bourgeois power.

DEU.name: German states / Thirty Years’ War arena
DEU.leaders: Ferdinand II; Gustavus Adolphus (as intervention); Wallenstein; Peace of Westphalia princes.
DEU.religion: Catholic, Lutheran, Calvinist legally recognized after 1648; enormous war trauma.
DEU.culture: Devastation and rebuilding; early Pietism seeds; territorial absolutisms.
DEU.story: The Thirty Years’ War — Europe’s dress rehearsal for total war — ends in Westphalia’s patchwork peace that teaches cuius regio on a ruined map.

AUT.name: Habsburg Austria
AUT.conflicts: Ottoman wars (Vienna 1683 arc); rivalry with France.
AUT.culture: Court at Vienna; Ottoman wars (1683 still ahead of/around long 17th c.).
AUT.story: The 1683 relief of Vienna becomes Habsburg Christendom’s last great cavalry epic.

SWE.name: Swedish Empire
SWE.conflicts: Wars in Germany, Poland, Russia; Baltic dominance struggle.
SWE.leaders: Gustavus Adolphus; Christina; Charles X/XI beginnings.
SWE.culture: Military innovation; Baltic empire; Uppsala learning.
SWE.story: Gustavus Adolphus — ‘Lion of the North’ — dies at Lützen as Sweden briefly decides Germany’s fate.

DNK.name: Denmark–Norway
DNK.conflicts: Wars with Sweden for Baltic supremacy.
DNK.story: Christian IV’s wars and building spree — ambition that overreaches against rising Sweden.

POL.name: Poland–Lithuania (PLC)
POL.conflicts: Wars with Sweden, Russia, Ottomans; mid-century Deluge.
POL.leaders: Sigismund III Vasa; Władysław IV; John II Casimir (Deluge era).
POL.religion: Catholic Counter-Reformation strengthening; Orthodox and Protestant nobles under pressure.
POL.culture: Sarmatian noble ideology; elected monarchy; huge multiethnic realm.
POL.story: The mid-17th-century Deluge — Swedish invasion devastating the Commonwealth — marks the turn from golden liberty to long decline.

RUS.name: Tsardom of Russia
RUS.conflicts: Polish wars; conquest of khanates; Baltic ambitions.
RUS.leaders: Boris Godunov; Time of Troubles claimants; Romanov founding (Michael).
RUS.religion: Orthodox; patriarchal institution; Uniate conflict to the west.
RUS.culture: After Troubles consolidation; icons and bells; serfdom hardening.
RUS.story: The Time of Troubles — famine, false Dmitrys, Polish occupation of Moscow — ends with a new Romanov dynasty elected from desperation.

TUR.name: Ottoman Empire
TUR.conflicts: Wars with Habsburgs, Safavids, Venice; Mediterranean & Balkan control.
TUR.leaders: Ahmed I; Köprülü viziers later; sultans of the post-Süleyman plateau.
TUR.culture: Tulip-era still ahead; classical Ottoman architecture’s afterglow; Mediterranean and Central European war rhythm.
TUR.story: Ottoman pressure and Habsburg defense set the tempo of southeastern European life long after Süleyman’s death.

ITA.name: Spanish/Austrian Italy & states
ITA.leaders: Spanish viceroys; popes; Savoy dukes; Venetian doges.
ITA.culture: Baroque art and music; Galilean science under constraint.
ITA.story: Galileo’s trial becomes modernity’s parable of science vs authority — more complicated historically, irresistible as story.

IRL.name: Tudor Ireland
IRL.summary: Surrender-and-regrant and plantation beginnings aim to anglicize Gaelic lordships; resistance culminates later in the Nine Years’ War.
IRL.conflicts: Desmond rebellions; Shane O’Neill; crown vs Gaelic alliances.
IRL.leaders: Tudor deputies; Shane O’Neill; earls of Desmond; Hugh O’Neill (later).
IRL.religion: Catholic population under a Protestant state church newly claimed.
IRL.culture: Gaelic learned orders under pressure; Pale Englishness vs Gaelic polarity hardening.
IRL.story: Ireland becomes England’s first long colonial laboratory — Reformation plus conquest, with consequences lasting centuries.

NOR.name: Norway under Denmark
NOR.summary: A kingdom without its own resident dynasty; Reformation arrives via Copenhagen.
NOR.conflicts: Danish governors; trade under Hansa then Danish control.
NOR.culture: Continuing vernacular life; loss of archbishopric independence.
NOR.story: Norway’s Reformation is an email from Copenhagen — institutional change without a local Luther.

BEL.name: Southern Netherlands (Spanish)
BEL.summary: The Catholic southern provinces reconquered by Parma remain under Spanish Habsburgs as Antwerp’s golden age wanes.
BEL.conflicts: Dutch Revolt warfare; religious cleansing northward migration of Protestants.
BEL.leaders: Duke of Parma (Alexander Farnese); Spanish governors.
BEL.culture: Flemish painting still luminous; commercial shift toward Amsterdam.
BEL.story: Antwerp’s fall and Protestant exodus help invent Amsterdam’s boom — a tale of two Low Countries.

CHE.name: Swiss Confederation (Reformation)
CHE.summary: Zwingli’s Zurich and Calvin’s Geneva make Switzerland a laboratory of Reformed religion beside Catholic cantons.
CHE.conflicts: Kappel wars between confessions; mercenary export continues.
CHE.leaders: Ulrich Zwingli; John Calvin; Catholic Waldstätten elites.
CHE.religion: Reformed vs Catholic cantonal split — a miniature Europe.
CHE.culture: Disciplined consistory religion; citizen-soldier myth; printing.
