CHE.story: Calvin’s Geneva — refuge for exiles and exporter of pastors — punches far above its Alpine weight in Atlantic Protestantism.

HUN.name: Hungary divided (Ottoman / Habsburg / Transylvania)
HUN.summary: After Mohács, the medieval kingdom splits into Habsburg Royal Hungary, Ottoman central occupation, and the Principality of Transylvania.
HUN.conflicts: Ottoman–Habsburg wars; Transylvanian diplomacy between sultans and emperors.
HUN.leaders: Ferdinand I Habsburg; János Szapolyai’s line; Ottoman pashas of Buda; Transylvanian princes.
HUN.religion: Catholic Habsburg west; Protestant strength in Transylvania’s famous tolerance diet; Orthodox Romanians; Islam in Ottoman zones.
HUN.culture: Frontier fortress warfare; multi-confessional Transylvania as outlier.
HUN.story: Mohács (1526) — two hours that kill a king and shatter a kingdom — is Hungary’s national catastrophe date.

GRC.name: Ottoman Greece
GRC.summary: Greek lands under Ottoman provinces; Orthodox Patriarchate in Constantinople as millet head; islands partly Venetian.
GRC.conflicts: Venetian–Ottoman wars; local bandit/klepht beginnings; tax and conversion pressures.
GRC.leaders: Ecumenical Patriarchs; Ottoman governors; Venetian captains in the islands.
GRC.religion: Greek Orthodoxy under Islamic sovereignty; crypto-Christianity debates in places.
GRC.culture: Post-Byzantine painting; folk song; diaspora merchants.
GRC.story: The ‘secret school’ legend of keeping Greek letters alive under Ottoman rule is later nation-myth — literacy and liturgy did persist, unevenly, through church structures.

periods.label: Modern
periods.narrative: Nation-states, industrial demography, world wars, EU integration, and global migration. Present-day Europeans still largely occupy the WHG–EEF–steppe ternary forged before 1000 BCE, with medieval overlays and recent cosmopolitan urban ancestry. Political identity and standard languages change faster than deep genetic clusters — yet fine-scale ancestry remains geographically structured.
periods.culturesNote: European nation-states, post-imperial/post-Soviet east, EU — political map over deep genetic and older linguistic families.

iberia.description: Modern nation-states on Iberian deep history. Autosomal structure still shows north–south and west–east historical clines (including Basque distinctiveness). 20th–21st century immigration diversifies cities without erasing those clines.
iberia.ancestryNote: Present-day averages schematic; urban samples more globally diverse than hinterlands.
iberia.languages: Spanish, Portuguese, Catalan, Galician, Basque, etc.

britain.description: UK and Ireland. Fine-scale genetic structure (e.g. People of the British Isles) often echoes early medieval kingdoms more than Victorian counties. English globally dominant; Celtic languages in minority/revitalization contexts; recent global immigration overlays cities.
britain.languages: English; Welsh, Irish, Scottish Gaelic, Scots…
britain.linguisticNote: English as global language from this islands’ modern history.
britain.ancestryNote: Early medieval structure still readable; urban cosmopolitanism recent.

france.description: Centralized republic with persistent regional deep structure and languages under pressure from French. 20th–21st c. immigration diversifies metros. Genetics still track older north/south and peripheral patterns beneath national identity.
france.languages: French; Breton, Basque, Occitan, Alsatian…; immigrant languages
france.linguisticNote: Strong standard-language ideology; regional revitalization movements.
france.ancestryNote: Regional structure + modern migration in cities.

central.description: Modern Central European states after empires and 20th-century border violence. Ancestry continuous with early modern Mitteleuropa plus displacements and recent migration. National labels sit on older German–Slavic–Uralic (Hungarian) mosaics.
central.languages: German, Polish, Czech, Slovak, Hungarian, etc.
central.linguisticNote: Nation-state languages after Habsburg/German/Russian imperial frames.
central.ancestryNote: Post-imperial continuity + 20th c. forced migrations + recent immigration.

scandinavia.description: Denmark, Norway, Sweden, Iceland (and Finland as Uralic neighbor in the wider north). Deep continuity from Iron/Viking Age in Germanic Scandinavia; recent international migration in cities. Finland’s Finnish language is Uralic, not IE — important map-edge exception.
scandinavia.linguisticNote: IE North Germanic bloc beside Uralic Finnish.

italy.description: Political unification overlays a deep north–south genetic and dialect continuum that still structures variation more than the modern state alone. Italian standard from Tuscan; dialects remain strong. Recent immigration adds urban diversity.
italy.linguisticNote: Standard Italian over a dialect continuum.
italy.ancestryNote: Strong north–south cline (ancient/medieval); modern migration in cities.

balkans.description: Post-Ottoman and post-Yugoslav nations. Genetic structure is finely regional; religion and standard languages imperfectly match ancestry. South Slavic, Greek, Albanian, Romance (Romanian), and Turkish-speaking communities intertwine.
balkans.languageFamily: South Slavic + Greek + Albanian + Romance + Turkish
balkans.languages: Greek, Bulgarian, BCMS, Albanian, Romanian, Turkish, etc.
balkans.linguisticNote: A shatterbelt of national standards after Ottoman and Yugoslav frames; language and religion borders only loosely track ancestry.
balkans.ancestryNote: Local mosaics; nation averages hide village-scale history.

eastern.description: Poland, Baltics, Belarus, Ukraine, western Russia, and neighbors. Broad east–west genetic clines; steppe and forest histories still readable. 20th-century wars, deportations, and border changes move people; deep ternary ancestry remains the backdrop to modern politics.
eastern.languageFamily: East Slavic + Baltic + West Slavic + others
eastern.languages: Russian, Ukrainian, Belarusian, Polish, Baltic languages, etc.
eastern.linguisticNote: Imperial and Soviet language politics still shape the map.
eastern.ancestryNote: East Slavic/Baltic/West Slavic structure + historical minorities; modern upheavals.

periods.linguistics: State standards (and co-official minorities), immigrant languages in cities, English as European lingua franca. Families remain Indo-European almost everywhere, with Basque and Uralic (Finnish/Hungarian/Estonian) as major non-IE exceptions in this map’s frame.

FIN.name: Republic of Finland
FIN.summary: Independent since 1917; Nordic democracy beside Russia.
FIN.conflicts: Winter War and Continuation War memory; EU/NATO era security politics.
FIN.leaders: Mannerheim in founding memory; post-war presidents; contemporary cabinets.
FIN.culture: Sisu myth; design; bilingual Finnish/Swedish legacy.
FIN.story: The Winter War — tiny Finland holding the Red Army — remains the national epic of survival.

SWE.name: Kingdom of Sweden
SWE.conflicts: No war since 1814; regional diplomacy with Russia/NATO neighbors.
SWE.leaders: Constitutional monarchs; Social Democratic architects of the folkhem; contemporary coalition politics.
SWE.religion: Lutheran heritage under deep secularization; new religious diversity.
SWE.culture: Welfare model; design; non-alignment tradition under pressure.
SWE.story: The folkhem — ‘people’s home’ — is Sweden’s modern founding myth of equality, now debated in an age of migration and insecurity.

DNK.name: Kingdom of Denmark
DNK.summary: Constitutional monarchy; EU member; Greenland/Faroes autonomy questions.
DNK.conflicts: WW2 occupation memory; contemporary Arctic and migration politics.
DNK.leaders: Constitutional monarchs; Social Democratic and liberal PMs.
DNK.story: From absolute Sound Toll power to small-state humanitarian branding — Denmark’s modern art is reinvention.

NOR.name: Kingdom of Norway
NOR.summary: Independent from Sweden since 1905; oil-funded democracy.
NOR.conflicts: WW2 occupation; resource and NATO politics.
NOR.leaders: Haakon VII’s resistance symbolism; post-war Labor architects; contemporary cabinets.
NOR.culture: Oil fund ethics; outdoor life; oil-to-climate tension.
NOR.story: 1905’s peaceful secession and WWII’s heavy-water/resistance stories frame Norway’s modern self-image.

GBR.name: United Kingdom
GBR.conflicts: World wars; Ireland partition; EU exit politics.
GBR.leaders: Victoria to present constitutional monarchs; PMs from Gladstone/Disraeli memory to contemporary cabinets.
GBR.religion: Plural: Anglican establishment legacy, free churches, Catholic and non-Christian communities, widespread secularization.
GBR.culture: Industrial then post-industrial society; global English; welfare state and its critics.
GBR.story: From workshop of the world and empire to Brexit-era European renegotiation — continuity of parliamentary myth under radical economic change.

IRL.name: Republic of Ireland
IRL.summary: Independent after revolution and civil war; EU success story with partition’s open wound in the North.
IRL.conflicts: War of Independence; Civil War; Troubles in Northern Ireland; Brexit border politics.
IRL.leaders: Collins/de Valera founding rivalry; modern Taoisigh; Northern peace-process figures.
IRL.religion: Catholic society secularizing rapidly after scandals; pluralism rising.
IRL.culture: Literary revival legacy; tech multinationals; diaspora.
IRL.story: Easter 1916’s ‘triumph of failure’ and the Good Friday Agreement are twin modern Irish stories — revolution and hard peace.

FRA.name: French Republic
FRA.conflicts: World wars; colonial wars; EU core.
FRA.leaders: Republican presidents and earlier revolutionary/Napoleonic memory still structuring politics.
FRA.religion: Laïcité as state doctrine over Catholic heritage; growing religious pluralism.
FRA.culture: Republican school; universalist claims; global art/philosophy prestige.
FRA.story: 1789’s legacy — rights and terror alike — remains France’s master story, replayed in every crisis of the republic.

DEU.name: Germany
DEU.conflicts: World wars; Cold War split; EU/NATO central power.
DEU.leaders: Post-1945 democratic leadership in FRG/Berlin Republic; memory of Bismarck, Weimar, and Nazi criminality as negative foundation.
DEU.religion: Catholic/Protestant inheritances; large secular and immigrant communities.
DEU.culture: Social market economy; Vergangenheitsbewältigung; European integration engine.
DEU.story: Auschwitz and division, then Ostpolitik and reunification (1990): Germany’s modern identity is responsibility before glory.

ESP.name: Kingdom of Spain
ESP.conflicts: Civil War 1936–39; colonial losses earlier; Basque/Catalan tensions.
ESP.leaders: From Franco’s dictatorship to parliamentary monarchy (Juan Carlos → Felipe VI) and democratic parties.
ESP.religion: Catholic culture under rapid secularization; regional identities.
ESP.culture: Transition culture; autonomous communities; EU membership remaking economy.
ESP.story: The Pact of Forgetting and its unraveling — how a democracy buries and then reopens civil-war memory.

PRT.name: Portuguese Republic
PRT.summary: From authoritarian Estado Novo to Carnation Revolution democracy and EU membership.
PRT.leaders: Salazar as negative founding memory; post-1974 democratic leaders.
PRT.culture: Fado; Atlantic orientation; Lusophone world ties.
PRT.story: The Carnation Revolution (1974) — almost bloodless end to dictatorship — is Portugal’s gentle modern myth.

ITA.name: Italian Republic
ITA.conflicts: World wars; fascist period; EU founding.
ITA.leaders: Post-war republican politics; earlier Mussolini as negative founding memory; EU-era premiers.
ITA.religion: Catholic society and Vatican neighbor; secularization.
ITA.culture: Design, film, regional cuisines as soft power; industrial north / agrarian south historic split.
ITA.story: From Fascism’s fall and resistance myth to ‘il sorpasso’ and recurring political instability — creativity beside fragile parties.

POL.name: Republic of Poland
POL.conflicts: Partitions memory; WWII; Soviet domination; NATO/EU.
POL.leaders: Solidarność generation; post-1989 democratic leaders; EU-era politics.
POL.religion: Catholicism as resistance identity under communism, contested in pluralism since.
POL.culture: Romantic independence tradition; EU mobility; war memory (WW2).
POL.story: Shipyard strikes in Gdańsk (1980) begin the crack in the Eastern Bloc — a trade union that helped end an empire.

RUS.name: Russian Federation
RUS.conflicts: Chechen wars; Georgia 2008; Ukraine wars — ongoing regional conflict.
RUS.leaders: Soviet general secretaries in memory; Yeltsin; Putin-era presidency.
RUS.religion: Orthodox revival after Soviet atheism; minorities of many faiths.
RUS.culture: High literary canon; petro-state geopolitics; Soviet memory wars.
RUS.story: 1991’s flag over the Kremlin ends the USSR; the post-Soviet story is unresolved empire, oligarchy, and war — still rewriting Europe’s map.

UKR.name: Ukraine
UKR.leaders: Post-1991 presidents; Maidan-era civic leadership; wartime presidency.
UKR.religion: Orthodox jurisdictions in flux; Greek Catholic west; pluralism.
UKR.culture: Language politics; Cossack memory; European aspiration.
UKR.story: Maidan (2014) and full-scale invasion (2022) make Ukraine’s sovereignty the defining European story of the early 21st century.

TUR.name: Republic of Turkey
TUR.conflicts: Greco-Turkish war; Cyprus; Kurdish conflict; regional interventions.
TUR.leaders: Atatürk’s republican founding memory; elected governments; Erdoğan-era presidency.
TUR.religion: Secular republic over Muslim society; contested laicism.
TUR.culture: Between Europe and Middle East; Ottoman nostalgia vs republican modernity.
TUR.story: Gallipoli and the War of Independence found the republic; EU accession’s stall and Middle Eastern wars keep Turkey’s European question open.

GRC.name: Hellenic Republic
GRC.conflicts: Balkan wars; Cyprus; tensions with Turkey.
GRC.leaders: Post-junta democratic leaders; EU-era premiers through debt crisis.
GRC.religion: Greek Orthodoxy as cultural establishment; secular youth.
GRC.culture: Classical heritage tourism; shipping; crisis cinema and politics.
GRC.story: The 2010s debt crisis — austerity, protest, near-Grexit — tests whether European solidarity is real.
